It iterates over all points $(\theta_i, \rho_i)$ in the projection frequency space, searches for the nearest Cartesian pixel $(i,j)$, and applies FFT [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method 'applies FFT' as part of the iteration process over points in the projection frequency space. However, the evidence (Source [S1]) explicitly distinguishes between the reconstruction of the Cartesian grid and the application of the FFT. The text states: 'Pour reconstruire la grille cartésienne, il suffit de parcourir l’ensemble des points (θi , ρi ), de rechercher le point (i, j) le plus proche et de le mettre à jour si nécessaire.' (To reconstruct the Cartesian grid, it suffices to iterate over all points... search for the nearest point... and update it). It further clarifies that 'Comme la FFT retrouve l’image en O(N logN )' (Since the FFT retrieves the image in O(N logN)), implying the FFT is a separate step performed *after* the grid reconstruction to retrieve the final image, not during the iteration over the polar points. Additionally, the claim mentions searching for the 'nearest' pixel, whereas the detailed notes describe a bilinear interpolation using the four surrounding points, not just the single nearest neighbor (which is described as the 'most elementary' version, but the notes focus on the interpolation method). The primary discrepancy is the timing and role of the FFT.
